theme: The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 16 slowly. It is a short psalm of trust, and it ties closely to the land inheritance you read about yesterday. David uses the language of boundary lines and allotments, but he applies it to God himself. Notice the shift in the last verses to the hope of life beyond death.
settingTheScene: Psalm 16 is a “miktam” of David, a psalm of quiet confidence. It sits well with the reading in Joshua. After surveying tribal allotments and the Levites’ inheritance in the LORD himself, we find David using the same language: “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup.” The psalm also has a surprising ending. Peter quotes it on the day of Pentecost as a prophecy of the resurrection of Christ (Acts 2:25-31), and Paul does the same in Acts 13. So it is a psalm of David’s own trust in God, and also a psalm that points beyond David to the Messiah.
observation: David prays, “Preserve me, O God, for in you I take refuge” (v. 1).
“I have no good apart from you” (v. 2).
He delights in the saints in the land, “the excellent ones” (v. 3).
Those who choose another god multiply their sorrows (v. 4).
“The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot” (v. 5).
“The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, I have a beautiful inheritance” (v. 6).
“I have set the LORD always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken” (v. 8).
“You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption” (v. 10).
“In your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (v. 11).
interpretation:
Psalm 16 is a profession of contentment. David has examined his life, and he discovers that everything good in it comes from God. “I have no good apart from you.” That is the first big claim. He then applies the language of the land to the Lord himself: “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot.” A “portion” is a share of an inheritance, a “cup” is what one is given to drink, and a “lot” is the allotment of land. David uses exactly the vocabulary of the chapters you just read in Joshua, and he applies it to God. God is not only the giver of the inheritance. He is the inheritance.

The effect is a settled gladness. “The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places.” It is the speech of someone who has stopped comparing his portion with others. He looks at what God has given, and he says it is beautiful. This is the opposite of covetousness. Those who run after other gods multiply their sorrows, because they chase a portion that cannot satisfy.

David also has a practice. “I have set the LORD always before me.” The posture is a conscious habit of living with God in view. And the result is stability: “Because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken.” A person who keeps God before his eyes finds that circumstances lose some of their power.

Then the psalm turns upward. “My flesh also dwells secure. For you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption.” David is confident that death will not have the last word. Peter explains in Acts 2 that David could not be speaking only of himself, for David died and his tomb is still known. He was speaking as a prophet of the resurrection of Christ, “the Holy One,” who did not see corruption. Jesus is the one for whom this psalm is perfectly true. His body was laid in a tomb, but it did not decay. And because he rose, those who are in him share the promise of verse 11: “You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore.”
connection: The language of portion and lot draws on Numbers 18:20 and Joshua 13-19. Peter quotes verses 8-11 in Acts 2:25-28, and Paul quotes verse 10 in Acts 13:35. Psalm 73:25-26 expresses a similar delight in God as portion. The path of life recalls Proverbs 4 and Matthew 7:13-14, and the “fullness of joy” anticipates Revelation 21:3-4.
application:
Test your contentment. Where are you tempted to say, “If only I had…”? Pray through Psalm 16:5-6 and ask the Lord to make you glad in the portion he has given.

Practice setting the LORD before you. Choose one moment in each day, such as your commute or your lunch break, to pause and pray, “Lord, you are here.” See whether it changes how you handle that part of the day.

And give thanks for the resurrection. Because Christ was not abandoned to the grave, your own death will not be an abandonment either.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what it means that he is your chosen portion.
Ask him to teach you contentment in him and to keep him always before you.
Thank him for Christ’s resurrection and the hope it gives you.
